summary.text: Abstract algebra is the study of algebraic structures, which are sets with specific operations acting on their elements.
Algebraic structures include groups, rings, fields, modules, vector spaces, lattices and algebras over a field.
It grew during the nineteenth century from scattered facts in several branches of mathematics and was unified in the early 20th century into formal definitions.

paragraphs.heading: Sets with operations
paragraphs.text: Abstract algebra, also called modern algebra, studies algebraic structures: sets together with particular operations that act on their members. Groups, rings, fields, vector spaces, modules, lattices and algebras over a field are all examples. The name was invented early in the 20th century to set this subject apart from older algebra, especially elementary algebra, where letters stand for numbers in calculations and arguments. In advanced mathematics this outlook is now so basic that people just call it algebra, and the longer name turns up mostly in teaching.

paragraphs.heading: Seeing structures from above
paragraphs.text: Category theory offers one shared framework for studying properties and constructions that look alike across many different structures. Universal algebra, a related field, treats a whole type of structure as a single object. For instance, the structure of groups counts as one object there, known as the variety of groups.

paragraphs.heading: Equations in words
paragraphs.text: Before the 19th century, algebra meant the study of polynomials. Around 1700 BC the Babylonians could solve quadratic equations posed as word problems. Solving in words like this is called rhetorical algebra, and it was the main approach up to the 16th century. Al-Khwarizmi gave us the word algebra in 830 AD, yet his own work was written entirely in words. Algebra written fully in symbols came only with François Viète's New Algebra of 1591, and even that still spelled out some terms that Descartes later turned into symbols in La Géométrie in 1637.

paragraphs.heading: Rules without restrictions
paragraphs.text: Working with symbolic equations led Leonhard Euler, in the late 18th century, to accept roots then dismissed as nonsense, such as negative and imaginary numbers. Most European mathematicians pushed back against these ideas until the middle of the 19th century. George Peacock's Treatise of Algebra of 1830 was the first try at resting algebra purely on symbols. In his older arithmetical algebra, a − b only made sense when a ≥ b, but in his new symbolical algebra every rule held without limits, which let him prove laws like (−a)(−b) = ab. His argument had a weak spot, the problem of induction: √a√b = √ab is true for nonnegative real numbers but fails for complex numbers in general.

paragraphs.heading: Where groups came from
paragraphs.text: Several parts of mathematics fed into the idea of a group. Lagrange's 1770 work on the solutions of the quintic equation gave rise to the Galois group of a polynomial, and Klein's 1872 Erlangen program in geometry led to symmetry groups. In 1832 Galois became the first to use the word group, for a collection of permutations closed under composition. The general idea took shape slowly through the mid-19th century: Arthur Cayley in 1854 described a group as a set with an associative operation and an identity, and in 1882 Walther von Dyck was the first to demand inverse elements as part of the definition.

paragraphs.heading: From scattered facts to axioms
paragraphs.text: Abstract algebra arose in the 19th century as harder problems and new ways of solving them appeared, with examples drawn from number theory, geometry, analysis and the solving of equations. Most of its theories began as loose collections of facts from different branches, gathered around a shared theme, and were finally unified by a common set of ideas. That unification happened in the first decades of the 20th century and produced formal axiomatic definitions of groups, rings and fields. Well-known textbooks, van der Waerden's Moderne Algebra among them, run almost the other way: each chapter opens with a formal definition and only then gives concrete examples.
